note: Single-pass extraction by Claude reading the paper text; evidence references sections/figures/tables. No multi-run validation.

components.description: Representation criteria and theory lead to empirical findings on representations, selection algorithms and pruning performance

nodes.name: Data pruning decomposes into two components
nodes.description: Data pruning methods decompose into (1) obtaining instance representations from a reference model and (2) a selection algorithm guided by an objective (difficulty, diversity or relevance to validation data).

nodes.name: Three criteria for good representations
nodes.description: Good representations should yield distances that (1) account for distance to the decision boundary, (2) contain label information, and (3) are more discriminative for important instances near the decision boundary.

nodes.name: Losses add boundary distance over hidden states
nodes.description: Compared with hidden-state distances, loss-based distances additionally integrate instances' distances to the decision boundary.

nodes.name: Only gradients are label-aware
nodes.description: Gradient-based distances further reflect label agreement, so only gradients are label-aware; losses and gradients are thus stronger than hidden states for identifying instances that are similar for training.

nodes.name: Representations influence selection more than algorithms
nodes.description: Different selection algorithms using the same representation overlap more in selected instances than the same algorithm with different representations (e.g. gradient-based proto-difficulty overlaps 0.79 with LESS-relevance on CAD but 0.26 with hidden-state proto-difficulty).

nodes.name: Gradient and loss selections overlap
nodes.description: Selections based on gradients and losses overlap more with each other than with hidden-state selections, as large as 0.75 for the same algorithm on CAD, consistent with the theory.

nodes.name: Algorithms do not follow their objectives
nodes.description: Selection algorithms do not always follow their intended objectives: hidden-state Prototypicality, aimed at difficult instances, mostly selects easy, correctly predicted instances far from the decision boundary on synthetic data.

nodes.name: Same-objective algorithms select differently
nodes.description: Algorithms with the same difficulty objective (hidden-state Prototypicality vs loss hard-to-learn) select vastly different instances, with NLP overlap ratios close to the random baseline.

nodes.name: Hidden-state methods are weak
nodes.description: Hidden-state-based pruning methods perform worse than or similar to random selection on all tasks, especially at low data budgets.

nodes.name: Difficulty methods need larger budgets
nodes.description: Hard-to-learn and self-influence are competitive with random only with data budgets above 30% and comparable to the dummy baseline at lower budgets.

nodes.name: Gradient methods are competitive
nodes.description: Gradient-based methods like LESS and self-influence perform competitively across most tasks, reaffirming the effectiveness of gradients as representations.

isolated_nodes.name: LESS needs label matching on imbalanced data
isolated_nodes.description: LESS performs well on highly imbalanced datasets only with label matching; otherwise it over-selects majority-label instances.

isolated_nodes.name: No algorithm wins everywhere
isolated_nodes.description: Different selection algorithms excel in different settings, and none consistently outperforms the others; maximizing relevance to validation data excels under substantial train-test distribution shift.

isolated_nodes.name: Methods fail outside original context
isolated_nodes.description: Data pruning methods applied outside their original context are often outperformed by random selection.

isolated_nodes.name: Hardest instances alone block convergence
isolated_nodes.description: Selecting only the hardest instances will make models fail to converge.

isolated_nodes.name: Prior studies treated methods as units
isolated_nodes.description: Previous studies typically treated data pruning methods as cohesive units, so the impact of individual design choices was unclear.

structural_reasoning: Theory about representations (Sec 3.1) predicts the empirical overlap and performance findings; the objective-compliance finding is separate but supports the budget-sensitivity result.
